issues.legal_issue: An earlier order directing an inquiry does not undo a completed urgent acquisition or restore land already vested in the government unless it sets aside the completed acquisition and vesting.
material_facts: The government invoked urgency powers and dispensed with an inquiry before acquisition.

Possession was taken under the urgent acquisition procedure, the land vested absolutely in the government, and possession was delivered to the acquiring market body before the landowners filed their petitions.
The earlier court order set aside the direction dispensing with the inquiry and directed an inquiry, but did not set aside the completed acquisition or restore the land.
An inquiry and a further declaration were subsequently undertaken on the assumption that the earlier order had undone the completed acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The earlier acquisition and vesting remained unaffected; the later inquiry and declaration were superfluous, and any award was to be treated as based on the earlier acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, possession may be taken in an urgent acquisition before an award, and taking possession vests the land absolutely in the government free from encumbrances. Section 6(3) makes the declaration conclusive evidence that the land is needed for a public purpose. Since the completed acquisition had vested the land, the later order directing an inquiry did not, without setting aside that vesting and restoring the land, make the land available for a fresh acquisition. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: acquisition_proceeding and urgent_possession_taken and land_vested_before_earlier_court_order and earlier_order_did_not_undo_completed_acquisition

predicates.acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerned the acquisition of land for a public purpose.
predicates.urgent_possession_taken: The government took possession under an urgent acquisition procedure before an award was made.
predicates.land_vested_before_earlier_court_order: The land had vested in the government before the court made the earlier order.
predicates.earlier_order_did_not_undo_completed_acq: The earlier court order directed a further inquiry but did not set aside the completed acquisition or restore the land.

issues.definition: When an urgent public-purpose acquisition has resulted in possession and vesting before an earlier court order that leaves the completed acquisition intact, the completed acquisition remains effective.

issues.legal_issue: A later declaration made beyond the applicable time limit need not be quashed when an earlier acquisition of the same land remains completed and effective.
material_facts: The original acquisition notification was published within the period to which the three-year limit in the first proviso to Section 6(1) applied.
The original declaration had been followed by possession and vesting before the landowners filed their petitions.
No court order stayed action or proceedings in pursuance of the original notification.
The later declaration was made beyond three years after the original notification, on the assumption that the earlier court order had undone the original acquisition and restored the land.
The earlier court order had not undone the completed acquisition or restored the land.
issues.conclusion: Although the later declaration would have been prohibited if the earlier acquisition had been undone and the original notification revived, the earlier acquisition remained effective, so the later declaration had no legal consequence and did not need to be quashed.
issues.legal_principle: The first proviso to Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 prohibited a declaration, for a notification published after the 1967 Ordinance and before the 1984 Amendment Act, after three years; Explanation 1 excluded periods during which a court stayed action or proceedings under the notification. On these facts the time-limit argument would have succeeded if the earlier acquisition had been set aside and the original notification revived. Because the completed acquisition remained effective, the later declaration was superfluous and had no legal consequence. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: acquisition_challenge_proceeding and earlier_acquisition_completed and later_declaration_after_applicable_time_limit and no_court_stay_period and earlier_order_did_not_restore_land

predicates.acquisition_challenge_proceeding: The proceeding challenged a declaration made in a land acquisition.
predicates.earlier_acquisition_completed: An earlier acquisition of the same land had resulted in possession and vesting in the government.
predicates.later_declaration_after_applicable_time_: The challenged later declaration was made after the time allowed for a declaration following the original notification.
predicates.no_court_stay_period: No court order stayed action or proceedings under the original notification during the relevant period.
predicates.earlier_order_did_not_restore_land: The earlier court order did not undo the completed acquisition or restore the land to its former owners.

issues.definition: When a later declaration follows an acquisition challenge, but an earlier acquisition has already been completed, the declaration is beyond the applicable time limit, no relevant court stay occurred, and an earlier order did not restore the land, the later declaration need not be quashed.

issues.legal_issue: A court is not obliged to entertain a fresh legal ground raised after avoidable delay in a challenge to a public-purpose land acquisition.
material_facts: The landowners raised the time-limit ground for the first time during their appeals in the High Court, although it had been available for nearly seven years.
The challenge concerned an acquisition for a public purpose, and setting aside such an acquisition could cause public expense and delay a project for the general public good.
The Supreme Court examined the ground to address the scope and applicability of the statutory time limit, while clarifying that this did not impose an obligation to examine late grounds.
issues.conclusion: The examination of the late ground did not establish an obligation to entertain such grounds; courts should be averse to entertaining acquisition challenges involving avoidable delay or laches.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles governing delayed challenges in proceedings under Articles 226 and 136 of the Constitution. A fresh legal ground is not governed by a different rule merely because it raises a question of law. In public-purpose acquisition challenges, avoidable delay or laches weighs against entertaining the challenge because setting aside an acquisition may waste public money and delay projects for the public good. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.acquisition_challenge_proceeding: The proceeding challenged a land acquisition.
predicates.public_purpose_acquisition: The acquisition was made for a public purpose and a project intended to benefit the public.
predicates.fresh_ground_raised_after_avoidable_dela: A ground that had been available earlier was first raised after avoidable delay.

issues.definition: When a delayed fresh ground is raised in a challenge to a public-purpose acquisition, the court is not obliged to entertain it.
